strengths: Strong empirical results: 77.84% on BIRD dev and 89.75% on Spider test represent meaningful improvements (5.55% over prior best open-source baseline), with comprehensive evaluation across multiple benchmarks

Thorough ablation studies demonstrating synergistic effects: Table 3 shows each agent is critical, with combined effect exceeding sum of parts; Figure 4 shows Validation Agent substantially outperforms alternatives
Well-motivated problem formulation: Clearly articulates three concrete challenges (compositional reasoning, schema understanding, environmental grounding) that justify the multi-agent approach
Solid technical execution: Clean three-stage pipeline with appropriate task decomposition; GRPO training choices are well-justified; thoughtful reward design with partial credit mechanisms
Comprehensive reproducibility: Detailed hyperparameters, complete prompt specifications, and commitment to code release support reproducibility and community usage
Detailed analysis of design choices: Figure 3 convincingly demonstrates impact of interaction turns; investigation of selection strategies provides insights into component contributions
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: Each major component (GRPO from Shao et al. 2024, ReAct from Yao et al. 2023, Generative Verifiers from Zhang et al. 2025b) is from recent prior work; contribution is primarily engineering-level combination rather than fundamental innovation

Missing computational cost analysis: Training requires 16 candidate trajectories per question, uses H800 GPUs, but no training time, memory requirements, or inference cost provided—critical for assessing practical deployment and reproducibility
Insufficient statistical rigor: No error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests despite modest test set sizes (1,534 BIRD dev examples); no report of multiple runs or variance analysis

Limited error analysis and failure mode investigation: No systematic breakdown of query types that still fail; no per-component error analysis; Spider-DK second-place result (78.13% vs 81.5%) and implicit domain knowledge gap unexplored
Arbitrary design choices without justification: Reward values (0.2, 0.1, 0.5) appear unmotivated; maximum turns T=10 chosen without comprehensive ablation; sensitivity analyses missing

Overstated generalization claims: All three agents trained exclusively on BIRD/derivatives; Spider is from same research community and era as BIRD, not true out-of-domain; Spider-DK results suggest model still struggles with implicit knowledge

Validation Agent training concerns: SFT on (trajectory, execution_result) pairs may suffer from distribution mismatch during inference; model probability calibration not verified; simplicity of prompt (Table 12) raises robustness questions

GRPO variance not addressed: Relative advantage computation (Eq. 4) uses small batch of G trajectories only; high-variance implications with sparse rewards not discussed; hyperparameter sensitivity unexplored
Unfair experimental comparisons: Closed-source baselines are API-based and not fine-tuned on BIRD, differing from open-source baseline setup; not true state-of-the-art on Spider-DK

Training data filtering unjustified: BIRD reduced from 9,428 to 8,036 samples without clear rationale; potential selection bias not discussed; Grounding Agent augmented to 90,102 instances with unclear methodology impact

strengths: Strong empirical results achieving state-of-the-art: 77.84% on BIRD-dev (5.55% improvement over next best open-source method), 89.75% on Spider-test, and 78.13% on Spider-DK, with effective cross-domain generalization without Spider training data

Well-motivated architectural design with clear problem decomposition addressing three distinct challenges (compositional reasoning, schema understanding, environmental grounding) through specialized agents

Comprehensive experimental evaluation including thorough ablation studies demonstrating component criticality, synergistic effects (Table 3), systematic analysis of interaction turns (Table 10), and multiple selection method comparisons (Figure 4)
Technical soundness with clear MDP formulation, well-grounded GRPO training with execution-based rewards, and elegant reframing of selection as next-token prediction probability

Strong reproducibility practices: detailed hyperparameters in appendices, explicit code release commitment, clear prompt templates, and use of standard public benchmarks with high schema grounding performance (97.78% recall, 90.74% precision)
Effective presentation with clear problem motivation, concrete examples (Figure 1), well-structured methodology, and comprehensive supplementary materials
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: GRPO is existing (Shao et al., 2024), ReAct is existing (Yao et al., 2022), generative verifiers recently proposed (Zhang et al., 2025b); primary contribution is engineering and task-specific application rather than algorithmic innovation

Critical missing practical deployment analysis: no reporting of absolute training time, inference latency, computational cost, or accuracy-latency tradeoffs; inference requires 8× computations for reported accuracy but cost implications not discussed

Data concerns: BIRD training set filtered from 9,428 to 8,036 examples using GPT-4o/Gemini-2.5-pro with unanalyzed impact on diversity; potential distribution shift in Validation Agent training on generator-produced trajectories with no cross-method generalization analysis

Absent error analysis: no categorization of error types, no examples of failure cases, no systematic investigation of what query types remain challenging despite 77.84% accuracy; limits understanding of remaining limitations

Prompt robustness not examined: system relies on carefully crafted lengthy prompts (Appendices D, E, H) with no ablation on prompt sensitivity or analysis of generalization to prompt reformulations; raises generalization concerns
Statistical significance not reported: single-run results without confidence intervals, error bars, or multiple runs; standard requirement for competitive benchmarks
Limited baseline parity: most comparisons against models without RL training; no comparison with other RL-trained 7B models at similar scale despite claiming advantages

Incomplete schema grounding evaluation: Table 8 shows strong metrics but lacks comparison with other schema linking methods; unclear specific contribution to final performance; 97.78% recall still implies ~48 failures

Hyperparameter justification limited: design choices (T=10, group size G=128, learning rate 1×10⁻⁶) lack sensitivity analysis or ablation; unclear how sensitive results are to these choices despite reproducibility claims
Generalization scope limited to English Text-to-SQL domain; unclear if approach transfers to other code generation or structured prediction tasks; only evaluated within SQL ecosystem

strengths: Strong empirical results with SOTA performance on BIRD-dev (77.84%) and Spider-test (89.75%), with thorough comparison against diverse baselines including base models, closed-source systems, and open-source trained competitors

Comprehensive experimental evaluation including component ablations (Table 2), dataset-wide controlled isolation (Table 3), interaction turn analysis (Figure 3), and selection method comparisons (Figure 4), systematically validating all design choices

Excellent efficiency transparency: Appendix F provides detailed latency (22.12s), token cost (13,325 tokens), VRAM analysis (15-47GB depending on deployment), and normalized budget comparisons showing MARS-SQL outperforms baselines even under equal time budgets

Evidence that gains derive from the framework architecture, not parameter scaling alone: 21B ensemble reaches 72.10% vs. MARS-SQL's 77.84%; single-model multi-task SFT at 32B reaches only 57.82%, proving specialization matters

Principled problem formulation: Reformulation as interactive MDP grounded in ReAct is well-motivated; clear articulation of three challenges (compositional reasoning, schema understanding, environmental grounding) addressed by role specialization

Data efficiency substantiated: achieves SOTA with only 35k LLM-labeled examples and 13 hours training, vs. millions of synthetic examples for competing SFT approaches; RL-only generator contributes 2.89% improvement independent of selection

Exemplary implementation transparency: comprehensive prompts (Appendices M-O), hyperparameters for all agents (Tables 4-6), training data construction details, and analysis of learned efficiency (Table 21 showing reduced average turns post-RL)

Honest discussion of limitations and trade-offs: transparently addresses 21B inference footprint, 22.1s latency cost, that grounding matters more with larger schemas, and that Spider-DK performance (78.13%) is not first-place
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: contribution is primarily engineering-focused, combining established techniques (multi-agent decomposition, ReAct loops, GRPO, generative verifiers). No new RL algorithms, verification methods, or architectural innovations introduced

Unjustified design choices: (1) Grounding reward heuristic (max(0.5, |Cg|/|Cp|)) lacks justification; no ablation on reward scheme; (2) Sparse RL reward (1.0, 0.0, -1.0) has no comparison to shaped rewards or intermediate signals; (3) Training data filtering removes 8.8% by agreement of Gemini and GPT-4o without analyzing bias or what was removed

Insufficient statistical rigor: no confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests despite test sets allowing for uncertainty quantification (2,147 Spider examples); no variance analysis across random seeds or training runs reported

Incomplete failure analysis: no categorization of error types (schema hallucinations vs. logic errors); Spider-DK second-place result (78.13%) under-explored; 48 failed schema grounding cases on BIRD-dev (Table 27) not analyzed for root causes

Reproducibility limitations: code stated as available but URL missing from PDF; GRPO implementation details vague (group size, advantage computation in Eq. 3); no random seed specification; exact training schedule not provided; distribution mismatch risk for Validation Agent not addressed

Practical deployment concerns: 22.1s per-query latency is substantial and marginally better than GPT-5-thinking (15s); 'Fast' mode drops to 68.71% (9% loss); sequential execution assumption may not hold in practice; scalability to 100+ table databases unexplored

Inadequate justification for three-agent decomposition: no evidence comparing to two or four agents; component contributions vary across benchmarks (Grounding more critical on BIRD-dev), suggesting decomposition isn't universally optimal

Speculative claims: Appendix E.2 claims SFT would need '15 million examples and 3-4 months' without evidence; confidence calibration of Validation Agent not analyzed; state space efficiency (exponential complexity risk) not discussed

strengths: Strong empirical results: Achieves 77.84% on BIRD-dev (5.55% over next best open-source), 89.75% on Spider-test (SOTA), with excellent out-of-domain generalization to Spider-DK and SParC without in-domain training
Novel training paradigm: First to make multi-agent Text-to-SQL workflows trainable via RL with execution-feedback rewards, moving beyond static prompting/SFT approaches

Comprehensive experimental validation: Thorough ablations (Tables 2-3, 23), controlled isolation analysis, parameter scaling experiments, and selection method comparisons demonstrating architectural gains beyond parameter scaling
Data efficiency: Achieves SOTA with only ~35k training instances in 13 hours, compared to competitors requiring millions of synthetic examples and months of training (Table 9)
Transparent efficiency analysis (Appendix F): Honest reporting of 22.1s latency, 13.3K tokens, and 21B parameter footprint; normalized budget comparisons show gains persist with equal inference time

Well-motivated three-agent architecture: Clear problem decomposition with Grounding Agent (schema selection, 97.78% recall), Generation Agent (error recovery via RL), and Validation Agent (trajectory selection with 97.15% selection accuracy on Spider-test)

Strong qualitative analysis (Section I, Appendix I): Detailed case studies showing learned sophisticated reasoning patterns including complex decomposition, data plausibility checking, boundary error recovery, and schema hallucination recovery
Excellent reproducibility: Code promised, complete prompts provided (Tables 26-31), hyperparameters fully specified, dataset construction details documented, implementation frameworks identified
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: Individual components are existing techniques (multi-agent decomposition, GRPO training, ReAct paradigm, generative verification); contribution is primarily workflow engineering rather than fundamental methodological innovation

Grounding Agent shows inconsistent gains: Improvement of only +0.46% on Spider-test vs. +1.04% on BIRD-dev (Table 2), making component benefits schema-dependent and of unclear utility on cleaner datasets

Incomplete mechanistic understanding: Paper demonstrates RL helps but lacks deep analysis of what specific error patterns are discovered versus SFT, what behavioral differences emerge, or whether behavioral cloning could achieve similar results
Inference cost remains substantial: 22.1 seconds per query with 13.3K tokens and 21B parameter footprint limits practical deployment; 'Fast' mode (3.1s) achieves only 68.71%, far below SOTA

Validation Agent selection gap: Best-of-8 accuracy is 83.76% but final selection achieves 77.84% (Table 25), indicating 5.92 percentage point gap; Pass@32 reaches 87.54%, showing significant unrealized potential

Training data contamination risks: Uses GPT-4o/Gemini filtering with potential data leakage; best-of-N/worst-of-N verifier training strategy could introduce bias; insufficient discussion of reproducibility without proprietary models

Limited systematic error analysis: No categorization of failure modes by query type/complexity; unclear which patterns remain problematic (nested queries, complex joins); error rates across difficulty levels missing
Statistical rigor gaps: No confidence intervals, significance tests, or variance quantification; single-run results for some experiments make robustness assessment difficult given typical RL variance

Reward design lacks ablation: Sparse {-1.0, 0.0, 1.0} reward signal; no exploration of finer-grained intermediate rewards or curriculum learning; justification for sparsity enabling diverse discovery is unvalidated
Limited scalability evidence: All experiments use 7B base model; Table 19 shows 7B→14B scaling gives only +1.55%; unclear how approach scales to 13B/70B models or if specialization remains beneficial

Conversational multi-turn understanding underexplored: SParC results (Appendix D) show improvement but lack analysis; unclear if gains come from model capacity vs. architectural innovation for context preservation

Comparison fairness issues: Closed-source baselines use different base models/training data; Arctic-Text2SQL-R1 trains on Bird+Spider; difficult to isolate method contribution from training data differences
